newsitem.title: RUSSIA: U.S-Russian space crew confident despite accident.
newsitem.headline: U.S-Russian space crew confident despite accident.

text.p: The three astronauts preparing to repair the damaged space station Mir looked well and confident on Sunday in their first television link with Earth since its accident in orbit.

"When we had problems with light and air conditioning, we were killing time by eating," commander Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, said when asked about reported problems with hot food after an unmanned cargo craft collided with Mir last Wednesday.
"Thank God, everything works fine now," he said with a smile to officials at Korolyov mission control, near Moscow.

He sat alongside flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39, and British-born U.S. physicist Michael Foale, 40, during the link. All three smiled and looked fit and at one point Foale put his arms around his comrades and praised their work.
"But even when things go wrong, it is great to work with these wonderful guys," he said.

Mir lost between 30 and 40 percent of its electric power potential in the collision with the cargo craft during a manual docking manoeuvre. The Spektr scientific module, which was already docked with Mir, was holed during the collision.
During the television link, which lasted about nine minutes, the crew took the camera around Mir to show some of the key points for the repair work needed to restore the power supply.
"We have been trained for all sorts of imaginable and unimaginable incidents and of course some of the elements of our training will be used in the work ahead," Lazutkin said.

"When we had to fight the loss of pressure after the incident (last Wednesday), I realised at some point that I was working automatically, without thinking. That shows that the training was really solid."

Foale, Tsibliyev and Lazutkin were due to check how Mir's batteries were charging and to try to increase the oxygen supply. Additional systems, including the toilet and the greenhouse, were being activated as the batteries charged.
Officials at the U.S. space agency NASA said in Cape Canaveral that a stabilisation system was now close to reactivation and life was slowly improving on Mir.
Five spinning gyrodyne devices which hold Mir's position had been reactivated and a sixth was expected to be operating soon, said Frank Culbertson, who oversees NASA's missions to Mir.
"What you have is a slowly increasing level of comfort on board and on the ground that things are returning to more normal operations," he said.
Russian officials said the Progress cargo craft which holed the Spektr scientific module in the accident would be allowed to fall from orbit into the Pacific Sea, possibly as soon as Tuesday.
The crew on Mir face risky repair work. The Russians will don spacesuits to enter Spektr while Foale sits in the escape capsule for safety.
They must install a modified hatch in Spektr's doorway so that cables can be connected to tap electricity from the module's solar arrays.
According to NASA officials, the crew will have to abandon ship if the hatch to Spektr cannot be resealed.

Vladimir Solovyov, who is responsible for flight coordination at mission control, said on Saturday a cargo craft would be launched on July 5 to take equipment to Mir. He expected the repairs to be done between July 10 and 14.

Despite a string of mishaps on Mir, NASA appears committed to sending astronauts to the craft. "Our current plan is to continue the missions. If something came up to change that assessment, we would certainly look at it very seriously," Culbertson said.
